extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century readers; writers of moral/character essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing moral, character-driven prose and essays that instruct or refine readers; includes principles for character portrayal, use of analogy, anecdote, and thematic classification. Useful for authors aiming to persuade or polish readers' minds through reflective prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways of influencing great people
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two Ways of doing any thing with great People, and those are by making your self either considerable or agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: The former requires finding a way to live without them or concealing need; the latter requires falling into their taste and pleasures. The text warns that agreeability often degenerates into imitation of faults, compliance, or subservience and can cost one virtue and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreeability vs. intrinsic worth
rubrics_metrics.description: To be agreeable to another, especially if he be above you, is not to be possessed of such Qualities and Accomplishments as should render you agreeable in your self, but such as make you agreeable in respect to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/antipatterns: Agreeing to another's tastes may force imitation of faults and loss of moral firmness; writers should show how characters sacrifice genuine qualities to please patrons or superiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extended analogy (sculpture/education)
rubrics_metrics.description: What Sculpture is to a Block of Marble, Education is to a Human Soul. The Figure is in the Stone, the Sculptor only finds it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, extended analogies to make abstract concepts concrete—show latent virtues being revealed by skillful cultivation; the analogy can structure an essay's opening and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral discourse as method
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourses of Morality, and Reflections upon human Nature, are the best Means we can make use of to improve our Minds, and gain a true Knowledge of our selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical aim: employ moral reflection and ethical discourse as the primary vehicle for improving readers' minds; the author explicitly declares this as the paper's purpose and frames subsequent content by it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast exotic examples with cultivated virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: I am much delighted with Reading the Accounts of Savage Nations, and with contemplating those Virtues which are wild and uncultivated... What Savage Greatness of Soul ... might be raised to, were it rightly cultivated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reports of distant or 'savage' peoples and striking contrasts to illuminate universal human potentials and to argue for the civilizing power of education; anecdotal exempla are employed to move readers morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shocking anecdote to illustrate a moral point
rubrics_metrics.description: We see in this amazing Instance of Barbarity, what strange Disorders are bred in the minds of those Men whose Passions are not regulated by Virtue, and disciplined by Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: present a vivid, emotionally charged narrative (e.g., the St. Christopher's tragedy) to dramatize consequences of unregulated passion and thereby strengthen the moral lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of the powerful's psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: The Great have one particular Privilege above the rest of the World, of being slow in receiving Impressions of Kindness, and quick in taking Offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization tip: depict elevated persons as proud, easily offended, and apt to despise old friends; such psychological traits explain social dynamics like favours, disappointments, and caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about patron promises and social advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: I have known of such as have been for twenty Years together within a Month of a good Employment, but never arrived at the Happiness of being possessed of any thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative realism: when depicting patronage or social mobility, emphasize the prevalence of false hopes, broken promises, and the long-term futility many experience; use such realism to critique social structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomize complex concepts for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame therefore may be divided into Glory, which respects the Hero; Reputation, which is preserved by every Gentleman; and Credit, which must be supported by every Tradesman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical device: break an abstract theme into distinct species or categories to clarify differences, tailor examples, and structure argumentation in an essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and reputation—avoid careless insinuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The most unhappy of all Men, and the most exposed to the Malignity or Wantonness of the common Voice, is the Trader. Credit is undone in Whispers... how careful ought a Man to be in his Language of a Merchant?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical writing practice: be mindful of the real-world consequences of speech and insinuation; authors should avoid careless or malicious remarks that can ruin reputations, especially of vulnerable social actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify 'quality' to inform characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: All Superiority and Preeminence that one Man can have over another, may be reduced to the Notion of Quality, which, considered at large, is either that of Fortune, Body, or Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this threefold schema (fortune, body, mind) as a toolkit for designing and contrasting characters—their sources of advantage will shape motives and behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical metaphor: act your allotted part well
rubrics_metrics.description: We are here, says he, as in a Theatre, where every one has a Part allotted to him. The great Duty which lies upon a Man is to act his Part in Perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/authorial counsel: encourage characters (and implicitly readers) to excel within their given stations; as a writing strategy, deploy the theatre metaphor to organize moral argument and character arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare authorial purpose to frame the work
rubrics_metrics.description: I have all along professed myself in this Paper a Promoter of these great Ends; and I flatter my self that I do from Day to Day contribute something to the polishing of Mens Minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing technique: explicitly state the essay's moral/intellectual aim to orient readers and justify selection of material; authorial modesty and appeals to correspondents can bolster credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn against servility to patrons and loss of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the Client ... has not only lost his Time, but also the Virtue which could render him capable of resenting the Injury which is done him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/plot device: depict the corrosive effects of seeking patronage—portray how dependence can erode integrity, leading to tragic or pitiable outcomes; use as cautionary exemplum.
